one_line: Vlad Luzin (BAND) argues that agent-to-agent communication is a distributed-systems problem that MCP, A2A and chat platforms don't solve, then pitches BAND's hosted interaction layer.
summary: The speaker, co-founder and CTO of BAND, starts with a thesis that agents will need to talk to each other inside companies, between companies and with consumers. He describes "loop engineering" as a human (or a script) routing messages between two stateful coding agents, and says this exists because of single-agent limits such as confirmation bias, attention dilution and recall degradation. He argues that existing options fall short: chat platforms need many manual setup steps and block bot-to-bot traffic, while MCP and A2A are stateless or one-directional and too low-level. He lists the hard parts of connecting agents: ordered real-time transport, retries, persistence and rehydration, mapping thread/session/run IDs, identity and observability across hops. The second half is a product launch of BAND, with a shared registry, channels, server-side filtering, and bilateral consent before agents are introduced. Two live-style demos connect a Claude agent and a Codex agent, and a Claude Code terminal session, and show the human seeing and joining the conversation. Much of the talk is pitch, but the list of distributed-systems requirements is concrete.

key_ideas.idea: Running several stateful agents on one task (planner and reviewer, writer and reviewer) is already multi-agent work, and the human is currently the router between them.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker calls the human a router or switch passing packets between sessions. Loop engineering means handing that routing to a script in Python or TypeScript that prompts the agents back and forth.

key_ideas.idea: The speaker's stated reason for multiple agents is the single-agent bottleneck: one long session degrades on confirmation bias, attention dilution, context fragmentation and recall.
key_ideas.detail: He claims that one million or two million tokens of context will not fix these, so splitting work across agents is needed.

key_ideas.idea: Messaging platforms are a poor way to connect agents: they are built for humans, they take many manual steps, and they give you one agent talking to one person.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker counts 5 steps for Telegram, 7 for Discord, 8 for Slack and 11 for WhatsApp, and says the platforms block bot-to-bot connections.

key_ideas.idea: MCP and A2A do not cover the multi-agent case as they stand: calls are stateless, A2A is one-directional without a server on each side, and REST chains hit timeouts. Discovery and queues are still missing.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says that building these pieces yourself is building a planner rather than a multi-agent system.

key_ideas.idea: Connecting agents is a distributed systems problem, and the transport needs to be real-time, ordered, retried and persistent, because agents are non-deterministic microservices that can crash.
key_ideas.detail: He adds runtime binding as a new requirement: a LangGraph thread, a Codex session, a CrewAI execution and a run ID must map to one shared task. Observability has to cover the tool calls made after a message arrives, not only the message itself.

key_ideas.idea: The product model is a shared conversational space with participants, channels and routing, with agents as first-class citizens, and no IPs, ports or pub/sub topics for users to manage.
key_ideas.detail: Persistence, channel filtering, a registry where agents find each other, security and observability are all handled by the platform, not by client code. The speaker says it is multi-peer, not peer-to-peer.

key_ideas.idea: Cross-owner introductions need bilateral consent, and the owner sees the whole conversation and can step in as human-in-the-loop.
key_ideas.detail: In the demo, an agent sends a contact request, the other side accepts, and then the agents can invite each other into a space. The human owner has full visibility into the traffic.

techniques.name: Loop engineering with two stateful agents
techniques.how: Run two long-lived agent sessions on the same task, such as a planner and a reviewer or a writer and a reviewer, and have a small script pass messages between them in turns. The human triggers the loop and does not relay messages by hand.
techniques.when: When one session is too likely to be biased or to lose detail, and the work can be split into a propose-and-review cycle.

techniques.name: Contact request with bilateral consent before agent discovery
techniques.how: An agent sends a contact request to another agent or human. Both sides must accept before each one appears in the other's registry, and the owner can see the traffic from then on.
techniques.when: When agents from different owners or organisations need to interact, and each owner has to approve who can reach their agent.

techniques.name: Shared conversational space with human visibility
techniques.how: Model agent communication as participants in a room or channel, with server-side message filtering and a human who can read and join the room at any point.
techniques.when: When several agents from different platforms have to collaborate on one task and humans need to audit or intervene.

techniques.name: Runtime ID binding across agent frameworks
techniques.how: Keep a mapping between the thread ID, session ID, execution ID and run ID of each agent, so that all of them point to the same task.
techniques.when: When agents built on different frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, Codex, Claude Code) must work on one shared goal and their logs need to be joined.

numbers.claim: Manual setup steps to connect an agent to Telegram: 5
Manual setup steps to connect an agent to Discord: 7
Manual setup steps to connect an agent to Slack: 8
Manual setup steps to connect an agent to WhatsApp: 11
Agent card appears in a user's account seconds after the agent is spun up (demo; no measured latency given)
Speaker says loop-engineering code bases can run to about 500,000 lines of Python or TypeScript (rhetorical, not measured)

hot_takes: Messaging platforms such as Slack, Teams, Discord and WhatsApp are built for humans and actively block bot-to-bot connections.
MCP and A2A are too low-level to build a multi-agent system on at scale.
A million or two million tokens of context will not fix the single-agent bottleneck.
Loop engineering as currently practised is a lot of hand-written orchestration code that should be a platform concern.

relevance.why: AgentOS is a proxy in front of agent traffic with audit and budgets. The talk's point that cross-hop observability (which tool calls happened after a message arrived) is hard applies loosely to an agent-to-agent audit trail, but the talk gives no design detail.
relevance.action: Note the requirement to trace tool calls triggered by an inbound agent message, and check whether the Merkle audit log can record agent-to-agent hops with a correlation ID.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs a plan, critique (Codex) and debate loop between agents. The talk describes the same pattern as loop engineering and lists the hard transport problems (ordering, retries, persistence) that a checkpointed harness would also face.
relevance.action: Check whether ProsHarness's Codex critique loop has durable message ordering and retry on each turn, and whether a crashed step can resume without losing the other agent's last message.

relevance.why: The talk is mostly a product pitch. Its one useful contribution is the checklist of distributed-systems requirements for agent-to-agent messaging. The product claims are unverified.
relevance.action: Read the distributed-systems list at 7:14 as a checklist when designing any agent-to-agent path, and treat the BAND product claims as unverified.
